summary: Cedar Heights, a neighborhood community, is adopting smart technology through the Neighborhood Improvement Plans (NIP), led by the Cedar Heights Neighborhood Council with tech companies and local government. Initiatives include smart waste management, adaptive LED streetlights, real-time bus signage, smart irrigation, resident-operated surveillance, youth coding workshops, and health-monitoring benches. Residents share positive experiences, while forums and 'Tech Tuesdays' workshops help address challenges and build technology skills.
one_line: Cedar Heights uses the Neighborhood Improvement Plans to roll out smart waste, lighting, transit, irrigation, safety, education and health technology, with resident feedback and training.
key_facts: The Neighborhood Improvement Plans (NIP) were first outlined on September 15, 2023, in a Cedar Heights Neighborhood Council meeting led by Chairperson Emily Rodriguez.
The council was inspired by the difference technology made during the global pandemic.
The Smart Waste Management System uses AI algorithms to optimize garbage collection routes, reducing traffic congestion and carbon emissions.
Smart bins communicate their fill level to waste collection services; Linda Park says they have helped reduce littering.
Smart LED streetlights in Cedar Heights adapt based on movement and ambient light levels, increasing visibility and security.
Digital signage at bus stops gives real-time updates on bus schedules and routes; Sarah Thompson uses it to commute to her job at the local hospital.
Smart irrigation systems in parks use weather forecasts and soil moisture sensors to reduce water consumption.
The council approved a resident-operated surveillance system accessible only to registered community members.
The local community center offers coding and robotics workshops for youth; teenager Alex Johnson aspires to be a software engineer.
Smart benches with health monitoring let seniors such as war veteran George Blackburn check heart rate and blood pressure in parks.
The council held forums where residents like Naomi Williams voiced concerns, and said feedback led to continuous improvements.
Regular 'Tech Tuesdays' workshops teach residents to use the new systems; octogenarian Betty Olson said they helped her overcome her fear of technology.
The NIP is ongoing and described as a journey rather than a destination.
